sections.h2: Selling in Bismarck: the lay of the land
sections.html:
North Dakota's capital city sits on the Missouri River's east bank, facing Mandan, and serves as the Burleigh County seat. Its 36.5 square miles rise to 1,745 feet. Median household income reached $73,877 in 2024, and the state government, Sanford Health and Bismarck Public Schools lead local hiring, so plenty of sellers are working around a job change or a retirement date.

Age separates one neighborhood from another, and buyers price accordingly:

  • Near downtown, the Cathedral District has homes dating to the 1880s and elm-lined streets.
  • The south side built up quickly after Garrison Dam improved flood control in 1953.
  • Newer growth runs north, near the shopping centers.

On the oldest blocks, you may find original plumbing, knob-and-tube wiring or tired foundations, and those repairs are what bog down an ordinary listing. Homes on the newer north and south edges more often carry special assessments for street and utility work.

Because Mandan is a short drive across the river but in Morton County, check the county and city of your parcel before searching for tax or permit records.

Winters in Bismarck are long, windy and snowy. January averages about 12.8 degrees Fahrenheit, the coldest reading on record is minus 45, and snowfall averages 50.5 inches a year. Roofs, furnaces and insulation take a beating season after season.

Expect inspectors to start with the roof, the furnace and the sump pump. An aging heater tends to lower offers. Seasonal flooding along the Upper Missouri continues, so a house close to the water should have its flood zone status checked ahead of a listing.

Think of a special assessment as your share of a public improvement that serves your block. The owner of record pays it on the same bill as the property tax. City Engineering picks the project and splits the cost among the parcels that gain from it.

How your share is measured varies with the type of work:

  • Storm sewer is measured by the square footage of your lot.
  • Sewer and water follow the front footage of your lot.
  • Paving and street lights are a flat charge per parcel or lot.
  • Sidewalk, curb and gutter depend on how much was installed.

Owners may clear the whole amount or spread payments across three to 15 years, depending on the improvement. Each year's installment shows on the tax statement and is paid at the Burleigh County Auditor's Office. Ahead of closing, ask the county for what is left. A buyer or title company will want that balance cleared or assigned in the contract.

January 1 is the nominal due date, but most owners pay half on March 1 and half on October 15. Clearing the full amount by February 15 takes 5 percent off. Real property is valued as of February 1, and the county mails bills around December 26.

DateWhat happens
February 1Assessment date for real property
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount
March 1First installment and special assessments due without penalty
April 1Deadline to apply for the Primary Residence Credit and homestead credit
October 15Second installment due without penalty

Payment options are the county website, the phone line at 1-800-272-9829, or a check mailed to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506-5518. Anything mailed without a postmark by the due date is late. Cards come with a processing fee.

sections.h2: What a Bismarck seller must disclose
sections.html:
An owner of a home with four units or fewer has to reveal material facts, meaning anything that could meaningfully change how an ordinary buyer would use and enjoy the place. When an agent handles the sale, the disclosure goes on a written form in the Real Estate Commission's format, and the buyer must have it before accepting the final purchase agreement.

Century Code section 47-10-02.1 carves out exemptions: sales by a fiduciary managing an estate or trust, transfers among close relatives and foreclosure sales. That is why inherited houses often change hands with fewer formalities. The statute gives buyers no private claim, though an agent who ignores it can be disciplined by the Real Estate Commission.

Closing costs here also benefit from the absence of any deed or mortgage tax in North Dakota.

Three paths lead to a sale: an agent, a private sale or a cash buyer. Each one costs you in time, price or certainty. Listing usually brings repair work, showings and a wait while the buyer's bank approves a loan.

  • An agent suits a house in solid shape when you can wait on a mortgage buyer.
  • A private sale suits you if a buyer is already found and the paperwork is no worry.
  • A cash offer suits a house that needs work, came through an estate, has tenants or faces a deadline.

Cash buyers take the house in its present state, so repairs and open houses come off your list. Whichever way you go, finish three tasks before picking a closing date:

  • Request a mortgage payoff statement.
  • Learn your special assessment balance.
  • Pull up the county tax record for this year.

Offers depend on the property, so we promise no price or timeline before seeing the house.

Plenty of local sellers inherited a house and live somewhere else. Selling it as it is works fine. Bring together the death certificate, the county tax record and any special assessment balance, and see an attorney about probate before a deed gets signed. Estate fiduciaries skip the written disclosure form, so paperwork is lighter, but telling the buyer what you know is still the right move.

An empty house keeps costing money. Tax and assessment installments continue to come due, and the furnace has to run through winter to protect the pipes. A cash sale with a set closing date can end those costs sooner than a listing that waits for a mortgage buyer. Many heirs also find that a quick sale spares them repeated trips to manage repairs from far away.

The path is similar for nearly every sale in town. Terms are agreed, a title company opens a file, and it requests your payoff from the lender plus tax and special assessment figures from the Burleigh County Auditor. If anything does not add up, it surfaces at this stage. On closing day the title company retires the loan, clears tax and assessment balances out of your proceeds and gives you the remainder.

Timing the sale around the February 15 and March 1 dates can change what you owe, since the discount and the first installment both fall in that stretch. If the house closes shortly after a due date, check whether that installment has been paid so it is not counted twice.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax on a Bismarck home sale?
faqs.a: Not from the state: North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Federal income tax on any gain is a separate matter, so talk to a tax professional.

faqs.q: Who owes the Burleigh County tax in the year a house sells?
faqs.a: The statement is sent to the owner of record. The closing statement divides the year between buyer and seller, so ask your title company how it will handle that.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Bismarck house with special assessments still owing?
faqs.a: Yes. Installments run three to 15 years and appear on the tax statement. The balance is paid at closing, or the buyer carries it if the contract says so.

faqs.q: Do I have to fill out a seller disclosure in Bismarck?
faqs.a: With an agent, you need a written disclosure before the buyer signs the final acceptance. Without one, you still must disclose material facts in writing. Estates and some family transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: What should I do with an inherited Bismarck house?
faqs.a: You can sell it as it is. Gather the death certificate, the county tax record and any assessment balance, and ask an attorney about probate before signing a deed.
